doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Short solos on 78s and Roy Haynes's audition with Lester Young
summary: Max Roach on record length limits, and Roy Haynes's audition story with Lester Young.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: That’s so interesting because also, those guys had to operate in a time when the length on a record was very limited.
They couldn’t go on and on and on.

Well Max Roach was telling me that when the 78s were, that sometimes you would only get four bars. And even in playing in the bands. And that’s what spawned a lot of the jam sessions because guys were frustrated because they wanted to improvise and stretch out more. But sometimes in a band you might have one tune that was your feature for that night, and if you acted up with the band leader you might not even get to play it that night. So then you’d leave there a nervous wreck. “I didn’t get a chance to really do my thing.” You know. And the thing is when you go back and listen to those records by the Freddie Websters and Lester Youngs, they didn’t play a whole lot of choruses. And Charlie Parker used to always say that. Leave them wanting some. Roy Haynes told me when he was first playing, was basically auditioning for the gig with Lester Young, he was playing and he was just slam-banging and everything and he was going through his stuff. He said Prez just kind of, he says, “No bombs, Prez, just tinti-boom, tinti-boom, and then waltz back out again and started playing some more.” And then after Roy settled down and started swinging behind him and just listening to him and playing to support
him then Prez kind of waltzed back again and said, “If you’ve got eyes, Prez, the slave is yours.” And that’s how he got hired with Lester Young.
